props.title: War of the Satellites

sections.content: War of the Satellites (1958) represents Allied Artists' rapid-fire response to Sputnik 1's launch, produced and released within months of the Soviet satellite reaching orbit. Roger Corman directed this Cold War-era sci-fi B-movie that captures American anxieties about the Space Race. Like Earth vs. the Flying Saucers (1956) and Invasion of the Body Snatchers (1956), it plays on fears of infiltration and cosmic threats, though with Corman's signature low-budget ingenuity. The film's aliens disguise themselves as humans to sabotage Earth's space program - a plot device that would later influence countless invasion narratives like They Live (1988).

sections.content: The late 1950s saw an explosion of space-themed B-movies responding directly to real-world developments in the Space Race. Missile to the Moon (1958) and The Cape Canaveral Monsters (1960) similarly rushed to capitalize on headlines, while more polished productions like Destination Moon (1950) had earlier set the template for "serious" space exploration films. Corman's film stands out for directly incorporating the Sputnik launch into its plot, making it one of the earliest examples of Cold War anxieties being processed through science fiction. SUBHEAD: Cold War Sci-Fi Themes

The film's central premise of aliens sabotaging Earth's space program reflects deeper Cold War fears about infiltration and technological superiority. Like Invasion USA (1952) and Red Planet Mars (1952), it merges the threat of communist infiltration with extraterrestrial invasion narratives. The rushed production actually works in the film's favor, capturing the genuine uncertainty and paranoia of the immediate post-Sputnik period. While crude by today's standards, its special effects by Irving Block (who also worked on Forbidden Planet (1956)) were innovative for their minuscule budget.
